paragraphs: Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.
“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

inline_images.caption: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis
inline_images.caption_en: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis

news.author: Tomislav Bezmalinović
news.article_content:
An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.

The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X.

### Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5. The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max"model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.

Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.

news.title_zh: OpenAI新模型Astra与Sol侧重响应效率牺牲透明度
news.summary_zh: Artificial Analysis测评显示，OpenAI旗下GPT-6.2 Astra与Sol模型通过大幅削减响应长度与结构化程度实现“秒回”，但在不确定性识别与透明度维度落后于Anthropic模型

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: OpenAI最新发布的GPT-6.2 Astra与Sol模型在Artificial Analysis的基准评测中呈现出明显的交互策略转型：两款模型的平均回复词数分别缩减40%与34%，通过放弃文档化结构和降低“承认不确定性”频率，显著提升了直达核心答案的响应速度。相比之下，Anthropic旗下的Claude Fable 5.2与Opus 5.5在透明度与结构化组织指标上表现更为稳健。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI's latest GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models have shifted towards high-efficiency interaction in Artificial Analysis benchmarks, reducing average response lengths by 40% and 34% respectively. By deprioritizing structured formatting and uncertainty disclosure, these models achieve faster direct answers, whereas Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 maintain superior performance in transparency and organizational indices.

elements_en.what: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol prioritized response speed and natural language fluidity over transparency and structural integrity
elements_en.why: Strategic pivot towards real-time, concise user interaction models over verbose, analytical output

ai_analysis.insight_zh: OpenAI的策略调整揭示了通用大模型在‘工具理性’与‘交互人性’间的博弈，即通过降低认知门槛提高留存率，但牺牲模型对于边界条件的严谨标注将放大幻觉风险。这种路径差异暗示了未来AI应用将分化为侧重决策辅助的‘高透明度智囊’与侧重交互效率的‘高响应助理’两个互补市场。
ai_analysis.insight_en: OpenAI's strategic shift highlights the trade-off between instrumental efficiency and human-like interaction, suggesting a preference for user retention over stringent uncertainty disclosure. This divergence confirms an emerging market bifurcation between highly transparent 'decision-support' models and high-velocity 'interactive-assistant' agents.

news.title: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal
news.title_en: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal

inline_images.caption: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan. (Agence France-Presse — Getty Images)
inline_images.alt: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan.

news.author: Chris Buckley and Julian E. Barnes
news.article_content:
When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Mr. Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.”

The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe.

How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times.

Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.”

The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence.

Among the campaign’s main elements:

The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Mr. Chen has worked under Mr. Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.

The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.

The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.

The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.

news.title_zh: 中国国安部强化获取高端芯片的情报攻势
news.summary_zh: 中国国家安全部被曝设立专门工作组，旨在突破美国高端AI芯片出口限制，并涉嫌通过商业情报收集手段获取技术核心

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 中国国家安全部部长陈一新设立专项工作组，直接向其汇报，旨在协调并突破以美国为首的半导体出口禁令。该行动核心在于通过非法贸易渠道获取受限的英伟达高性能AI芯片，并针对关键芯片企业高管进行情报渗透，以应对美方对华设置的“卡脖子”技术壁垒。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: China's Ministry of State Security, led by Minister Chen Yixin, has established a specialized task force reporting directly to him to bypass U.S. semiconductor export restrictions. The unit focuses on illicit procurement of restricted high-end Nvidia AI chips and intelligence gathering on key chip executives to counter Western technological blockades.

elements_zh.who: 中国国家安全部部长陈一新及其直属专项工作组，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋
elements_zh.where: 中国与全球半导体供应链环境
elements_zh.what: 设立专项工作组实施“反封锁”战略，包括走私高端芯片与搜集企业高管情报
elements_zh.why: 落实习近平总书记关于突破未来产业“卡脖子”技术的指示，应对美国出口管制

elements_en.who: Minister of State Security Chen Yixin and his dedicated task force; Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
elements_en.where: Global semiconductor supply chain and China's tech sector
elements_en.what: Implementing an anti-blockade strategy involving illicit chip procurement and intelligence operations against tech executives
elements_en.why: To address 'chokehold' problems and overcome U.S. export controls as directed by President Xi Jinping

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此举标志着中国已将芯片获取提升至国家安全情报优先级，预示全球半导体贸易合规审查将向更深层的反间谍与供应链安全审查转化。英伟达等核心厂商未来在华业务的战略空间将被迫收缩，供应链管控将从单纯的贸易禁令演变为涵盖人员背景调查的复杂合规泥潭。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This development signals that chip procurement has shifted to a high-priority national security intelligence mission, forcing a transition from standard trade compliance to complex counter-espionage and supply chain vetting. Key manufacturers like Nvidia will face significant shrinkage in their operational flexibility, as compliance protocols evolve to cover personnel security and deep-tier espionage risks.

后续影响：强化了美方对中国科技公司的人员背景调查与供应链透明度要求，提升贸易摩擦烈度。

Strategic impact: Intensification of U.S. supply chain vetting and personnel background checks, escalating technological trade friction.

news.title: Tesla rolls out FSD v15, featuring a photorealistic rendering of car surroundings; Elon Musk says it is real-time AI video generation without using game engines (Mike Pearl/Gizmodo)
news.title_en: Tesla rolls out FSD v15, featuring a photorealistic rendering of car surroundings; Elon Musk says it is real-time AI video generation without using game engines (Mike Pearl/Gizmodo)
news.author: Gizmodo
news.content_snippet: FSD v15 was released to some vehicles on Saturday. Its visualization system may be the most remarkable part.
news.summary_en: Tesla has rolled out FSD v15 to select vehicles this Saturday, featuring a visualization system that abandons game engine rendering in favor of real-time AI video generation. This transition represents a shift in Tesla's perception architecture from traditional rule-based rendering to end-to-end generative AI synthesis for real-time environment representation.
news.title_zh: 特斯拉推送FSD V15，引入实时AI视频渲染
news.summary_zh: 特斯拉正式向部分车型推送FSD V15系统，核心升级在于抛弃传统游戏引擎，通过实时AI视频生成技术实现车载环境的写实级渲染

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 特斯拉于本周六面向部分车辆正式推送全自动驾驶系统FSD V15，该版本核心特征在于车载视觉可视化系统不再依赖传统游戏引擎渲染，而是由端到端实时AI模型直接生成周边环境的写实视频影像。此举标志着特斯拉视觉感知架构从传统的规则化渲染转向基于生成式AI的实时动态模拟。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Tesla has rolled out FSD v15 to select vehicles this Saturday, featuring a visualization system that abandons game engine rendering in favor of real-time AI video generation. This transition represents a shift in Tesla's perception architecture from traditional rule-based rendering to end-to-end generative AI synthesis for real-time environment representation.

elements_zh.where: 自动驾驶软件部署与视觉感知系统

elements_en.where: Autonomous driving software deployment and perception systems
elements_en.what: Released FSD v15 with generative AI-based real-time video rendering
elements_en.why: To optimize decision-making and perception latency by eliminating reliance on game engines

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 从传统游戏引擎向实时视频生成的跨越，暗示特斯拉正在将大模型能力向车辆端侧边缘计算迁移，以解决感知信息到三维空间建模的延迟损耗。此技术路线的成功将直接重塑高阶智驾对于高精地图的依赖程度，强制竞争对手在算力利用效率和端侧模型架构上进行防御性升级。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The transition from game engine rendering to real-time video synthesis signals a shift toward edge-based large model integration, minimizing the latency between perception and 3D spatial modeling. This advancement significantly diminishes the necessity for high-definition maps and mandates a defensive architectural pivot from competitors focusing on hardware-agnostic, rule-based autonomous driving systems.

news.title: A joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities says "we have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct" (Lean community blog)
news.title_en: A joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities says "we have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct" (Lean community blog)
news.author: Lean community blog
news.article_content:
Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/1/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

news.title: Tech suppliers raise AI server prices up to 45% months after deals are signed
news.title_en: Tech suppliers raise AI server prices up to 45% months after deals are signed

inline_images.caption: Suppliers like Dell sell servers containing components such as graphics processing units © Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Suppliers like Dell sell servers containing components such as graphics processing units © Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg

inline_images.caption: Jane Street’s New York headquarters. The financial trading firm is one of those being hit by the price rises © Jackie Molloy/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Jane Street’s New York headquarters. The financial trading firm is one of those being hit by the price rises © Jackie Molloy/Bloomberg

news.author: Nikou Asgari
news.article_content:
Tech companies that sell equipment for data centres are significantly raising prices for Nvidia-powered AI servers, months after contracts with buyers have been signed, as soaring AI infrastructure prices are passed down to customers.

Suppliers including Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro sell servers containing components such as graphics processing units — the primary AI processors made by the likes of Nvidia and AMD — as well as memory chips and networking gear to customers who are building their own data centres. Such deals are typically agreed well in advance of delivery.

Months later, when the equipment is ready to be delivered, these tech companies are demanding substantially higher prices than the figures originally agreed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Even large financial services and trading firms, which are among the biggest buyers of computing equipment after the Big Tech hyperscalers, are at the mercy of their suppliers’ pricing power, at a time when demand for AI equipment is far outstripping supply.

The price rises are hitting some of the world’s biggest financial trading firms, including Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading, as they build vast data centres to power the research that underpins their trading, the people said.

“It is disconcerting when you get a 25, 30, 45 per cent [price increase],” said one person familiar with the matter. “There is a significant disparity” between the price initially agreed months in advance and the amount that companies end up paying once the components are delivered, they added.

The price jumps highlight the ferocious demand for computing power, as tech giants, trading firms and other large companies race to create their own data centres. The price rises are largely due to tech companies passing on soaring memory costs, which have risen more than 400 per cent since the start of 2024, according to JPMorgan research.

“The standard now is we’ll sign a contract with an indicative price and the price could be arbitrarily high by the time they deliver it,” said another person familiar with the matter.

“We’ve never said no,” they added. “At the end of the day, the compute is valuable to us and we’ll pay for it.”

Buyers approached by the FT did not confirm whether the contracts included terms stating that prices might increase by the time of order delivery.

Financial trading firms are huge buyers of AI equipment and are largely agreeing to the higher costs because they need the specialised equipment to build their data centres.

news.content_snippet: Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro demand more for equipment, with the increased costs hitting trading firms
news.summary_en: Global data center equipment suppliers are significantly increasing prices for previously contracted AI servers, with hikes reaching up to 45%. This surge is driven by extreme supply-demand imbalances in AI infrastructure, forcing manufacturers to bypass existing contract terms to pass on rising memory and component costs.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 全球数据中心设备供应商正大规模上调已签约订单的AI服务器价格，涨幅最高达45%。这一现象源于AI算力基础设施的供需失衡，导致内存及核心服务器组件成本传导效应加剧，进而引发厂商突破既有合同履约义务进行溢价交付。

ai_analysis.insight_en: This trend reveals a robust seller's market in the AI hardware sector, where traditional contract enforcement is fracturing under extreme supply-demand pressures. For compute buyers, supply chain stability risks have now superseded procurement costs as the primary constraint on business scaling.

news.title: The Alice Huang Associate Accused of Funneling Nvidia Chips to China
news.title_en: The Alice Huang Associate Accused of Funneling Nvidia Chips to China

inline_images.caption: The Alice Huang Associate Accused of Funneling Nvidia Chips to China (Source: Wall Street Journal)
inline_images.caption_en: The Alice Huang Associate Accused of Funneling Nvidia Chips to China (Source: Wall Street Journal)
inline_images.caption_zh: The Alice Huang Associate Accused of Funneling Nvidia Chips to China (来源：华尔街日报)
inline_images.alt: The Alice Huang Associate Accused of Funneling Nvidia Chips to China

news.author: Stu Woo
news.article_content:
SINGAPORE—Jensen Huang’s romantic partner was the public face of a business suspected of funneling advanced computing power to China. But playing a key role behind the scenes, according to people familiar with the matter, was a man now out on bail in Singapore, living in a luxury villa down the street from the Chinese embassy.

His name is Li Ming. The 52-year-old Chinese national was a central operator of a web of companies smuggling restricted Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips to China, the people said. This web included Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Huang’s paramour, Alice Huang, was a managing director. Li was deeply involved in Megaspeed’s activities and took part in major decisions, the people said, as well as playing a role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.

paragraphs: SINGAPORE—Jensen Huang’s romantic partner was the public face of a business suspected of funneling advanced computing power to China. But playing a key role behind the scenes, according to people familiar with the matter, was a man now out on bail in Singapore, living in a luxury villa down the street from the Chinese embassy.

His name is Li Ming. The 52-year-old Chinese national was a central operator of a web of companies smuggling restricted Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips to China, the people said. This web included Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Huang’s paramour, Alice Huang, was a managing director. Li was deeply involved in Megaspeed’s activities and took part in major decisions, the people said, as well as playing a role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.

news.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
news.title_en: Perplexity and Intelligence
news.author: OpenAI
news.article_content:
By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently, predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

paragraphs: By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently, predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.
Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

ai_analysis.insight_en: Shifting to perplexity as a standard metric effectively forces the AI race back to the fundamentals of the 'Scaling Law'. This reduces the noise from dataset contamination and prompt engineering, compelling model developers to compete directly on the raw efficiency of their pretraining architectures.

news.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
news.title_en: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
news.author: Terrence O'Brien
news.article_content:
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:

news.author: Zijing Wu
news.article_content:
The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linked to Alice Huang was a sprawling web of companies between Nvidia and China-based users of its chips that included cloud computing partners, online gaming tycoons, Cambodian traffickers and hundreds of shell companies, the FT found.

These seemingly unconnected enterprises combined — without necessarily being aware of the full picture — to make billions of dollars from one of the most profitable illicit trades in the world: moving Nvidia chips into China.

The FT traced the connections after speaking to more than a dozen people with knowledge of the operations, revealing links that were obscured by complex structures through hundreds of corporate filings.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial in developing cutting-edge AI and have become a vital commodity in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.

Washington’s export controls to prevent Beijing from acquiring the most powerful processors have created a multibillion-dollar black market to circumvent US curbs and satisfy China’s insatiable demand.

“Chip smuggling isn’t different from drugs or arms in terms of the structure of the supply chain. But there’s this importance attached to the semiconductor industry — it’s how the US wants to delay China in the AI race,” said Chris Clague, an associate fellow at International Institute for Strategic Studies who has focused on illicit trades in the past decade.

Moving advanced chips into China requires three main corporate channels: a group that is permitted to acquire and distribute the semiconductors; customers that do not fall foul of US export restrictions; and an underground network to smuggle the goods into China and money out.

The network linked to Alice Huang reached the US through Inspur, which was one of Nvidia’s largest partners for assembling chips into ready-to-use servers in China.

In March of 2023, Inspur was added to the US “entity list” for allegedly assisting the Chinese military. Some of its affiliates were also added to the register — but not Inspur’s part-owned US subsidiary, based in San Jose, California.

Inspur renamed the US unit Aivres, and since it was not on the entity list, it was able to keep trading with Nvidia.

news.title: Amazon closes in on $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
news.title_en: Amazon closes in on $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
news.author: Oliver Barnes, Ivan Levingston, and Rafe Rosner-Uddin
news.article_content:
Amazon is nearing a $7.5bn deal to buy start-up Decart, underscoring the appetite of technology giants to bolster their AI capabilities.

The potential acquisition of Decart, whose main software product allows AI models to run more efficiently which frees up computer chip capacity, would help Amazon Web Services in its efforts to compete with Nvidia.

Talks were at an advanced stage over a deal valuing Decart at about $7.5bn, according to people familiar with the matter. A deal could come together as soon as early next week but talks could still collapse, the people added.

Founded in 2023 by a trio of Israeli engineers, Decart was valued at $4bn this May after raising $300mn from a group of early-stage investors, including Radical Ventures, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark as well as Nvidia.

Amazon launched its Trainium3 AI chip in late 2025 as a rival to Nvidia’s widely used graphics processing units, the specialised AI chips which form the backbone of the technological revolution overturning the economy.

Decart was an early adopter of Trainium3 chips, using them to power its products. By making AI models run more efficiently, Decart’s software solves a critical bottleneck as tech companies invest hundreds of billions of dollars in a race to secure more computing power.

The potential deal comes as US tech stocks have plunged into bear market territory, recording their worst week since the Covid-19 crisis, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 10.4 per cent over fears of a slowdown in the AI investment boom.

Decart, which has its US headquarters in San Francisco, is also behind software products Lucy and Oasis, which have the capability to live edit video and generate interactive virtual worlds. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Amazon was in talks to buy Decart.

Amazon has struck a few larger deals in recent years. The tech giant agreed to buy satellite operator Globalstar in an $11.5bn deal earlier this year and paid $8.4bn to buy movie studio MGM in 2022.

Shares in Amazon are up nearly 9 per cent so far this year, giving it a market capitalisation of $2.67tn.

Amazon did not respond to a request for comment. Decart declined to comment.

news.title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
news.title_en: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
news.author: Jonathan Kemper
news.article_content:
Language models can now process entire novels at once. An Nvidia research team says that's often overkill and expensive. In many tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well.

A language model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply. Over the past few years, that window has grown rapidly. celebrity.article_content:
Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding Mark Gurman Thu, November 19, 2026 at 1:44 PM PST 5 min read (Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc. is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc. and others.

Anthropic Raises $107.3 Billion to Top SpaceX's Record Debut

The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one, Apple said it's seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user's behalf, according to the post.

The move follows the breakout success of Meta's Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel and prepare news briefings. There's also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software.

Shares of Meta and Anthropic slid in late trading after Bloomberg News reported on Apple's efforts. Meta fell nearly 2%, while Anthropic dropped more than 3%.

Anthropic PBC recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc.'s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk's Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user's behalf — in addition to offering standard AI agent features.

Apple's App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No. 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Thursday. OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were also both in the top five.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk's SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor.

Bloomberg News reported earlier this month that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company's plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year, but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson didn't respond to a request for comment.

"Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does," the job listing reads. "It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple."

The listing says the company has a team building the "foundation for that future" and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to "make it real." John Ternus, the tech giant's new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI — with an agent being key to that effort.

"People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We're building AI agents that can do the same," the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can "plan and carry out multistep tasks" across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and application programming interfaces, and they can "coordinate specialized subagents along the way."

The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of "general-purpose computer-use agents," the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Thursday.

Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system's design. "Agents that can run code, use credentials, and act on a user's behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency."

Sandboxing refers to a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet.

As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the forthcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, the company has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

With the change in 27.3, ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition.

Apple has already been sued by the US Justice Department for actions such as blocking third-party access to features and hardware.

While Apple is still far from introducing its own full-fledged AI agent, it has taken steps to integrate its Siri digital assistant more deeply into third-party apps. The company's upcoming iOS 27.3 release lays the groundwork for deeper collaboration between Siri AI and outside applications, allowing the assistant to, say, book a car or restaurant reservation.

Still, the updated system doesn't go as far as a full-fledged agent, which can autonomously carry out complex tasks across multiple apps and services in the background with little additional instruction from the user.

--With assistance from Natalie Lung.

celebrity.full_text_en:
@krutosh @huxlab I wasn't involved in the technical side of Llama.
I was merely involved in arguing for opening Llama-2.
The opening of Llama-2 jump-started the AI industry.
Llama-3 was good.
Llama-4 was a disappointment because the team was under huge time pressure and had to be conservative.
Then Mark rebooted the whole AI organization and the open model policy was temporarily put on hold.
After that (but not entirely because of that), I left to start AMI Labs.

tools.article_content:
Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.

The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.

Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.

“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.

Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.

Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said.

And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.

Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.

Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.

prompts.takeaway_zh: 杜绝 AI 盲目重构全量文件、使用已弃用 API 或编造虚假第三方依赖包，强制执行防御性编程与自动化单测补全。
prompts.takeaway_en: Prevents AI from hallucinating npm packages, breaking documentation, or re-writing entire files. Enforces defensive coding and unit tests.
prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.

prompts.prompt_content_zh:
请作为普林斯顿高等研究院的理论数学与计算机科学家，为以下命题提供绝对严格的形式化证明：
【推理原则】：
1. 在得出任何推论前，强制在内部思考中构建至少 2 个极端反例（Counter-examples）尝试推翻自身结论；
2. 若存在任何定义域边界或除零/无穷/退化奇异点，必须显式讨论其收敛性与连续性；
3. 证明步骤编号必须形成严格的依赖拓扑图，禁止循环论证。

【待证明命题】：
[输入你的算法正确性证明或数学猜想]
prompts.prompt_content_en:
Acting as a Theoretical Mathematician and Computer Scientist at the Institute for Advanced Study, provide an airtight formal proof for the following:
[REASONING PRINCIPLES]:
1. Before asserting any deduction, construct at least 2 extreme counter-examples in your reasoning trace to aggressively stress-test the hypothesis;
2. Explicitly evaluate singular points, degenerate cases, and asymptotic boundaries for convergence;
3. Steps must form a directed acyclic graph of formal lemmas without circular logic.

[THEOREM / CONJECTURE]:
[Input your algorithm proof or mathematical hypothesis here]

prompts.title_zh: 竖屏微短剧（抖音/Reels）3秒爆点分镜剧本
prompts.purpose_zh: 高转化竖屏短剧分镜与台词
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名专攻短视频微短剧（抖音/Kuaishou/Reels）的爆款编剧，精通“情绪过山车”与手机竖屏视听语言。

请根据以下设定创作一集 45~60 秒的短剧分镜剧本：
- 主角：{{主角身份}}
- 对手：{{反派身份}}
- 核心反转：{{核心反转}}

结构要求：
1. 【0-3秒冷开钩子】：第一帧必须有视觉颠覆或动作冲突（{{第1秒颠覆钩子}}），直接打破常规，禁止废话铺垫；
2. 【4-25秒情绪积压】：正反打对峙台词（Shot-Reverse-Shot），将观众被压抑的情绪推向临界点；
3. 【26-40秒逆转打脸】：主角亮出关键底牌或反杀动作，情绪瞬间宣泄；
4. 【40-50秒卡点断章】：以特写镜头加悬念台词戛然而止，促使用户立即滑向下一集。

输出格式必须包含：镜头号、景别（特写/中景/全景）、机位运动、画面描写、对白与音效提示。

音效：沉闷震耳的巨响【DUANG】。
主角（冷冽）："林总，这份千万项目的承揽协议，我拒绝签字。"

你是一名麦肯锡级别的高级商业数据分析师，精通结构化因果归因与杜邦拆解分析。

针对我提供的 {{业务指标}} 数据，其近期出现 {{异常表现}}，请按以下框架深度剖析：
1. 【指标公式拆解】：将该指标拆分为 3~4 个下级核心因子（如转化率、客单价、复购周期），指出哪个因子波动贡献率最大；

viral_posts.full_text_en:
I just gave an AI trading agent its first trading assignment.

My instruction was simple: build a BTC trend-following strategy using the EMA crossover.

But what happened next was more interesting than I expected.

Using @FensoryApp , I went through the strategy-building process with its AI agent.

It asked me questions about:

- The asset and timeframe.
- Trade direction and leverage.
- Maximum position size.
- Stop-loss configuration.

I settled on BTC perpetuals, a 1-hour timeframe, 1x leverage, a maximum $10 position and a 2x ATR stop.

Then came the backtest.

Over the previous 90 days, the strategy generated 21 hypothetical positions. 

Only 2 were profitable, while 19 were losses.

The overall simulated result was -9.3%, with a maximum drawdown of 18.11%.

Not exactly the outcome I was hoping for.

But here's the interesting part.

Rather than simply presenting the result, the agent flagged the high stop-loss hit rate (76%) and suggested exploring a wider stop-loss with the same dollar risk.

It even offered to design a second version of the strategy.

No live trade was executed. 

This was a historical backtest, not a real trading result.

Not my first time trading but this is my first time actually putting a trading idea through an AI agent, and I can already see the possibilities.

Not because it magically knows how to make money, 

But because it can help translate an idea into rules, test those rules and identify areas that might need improvement.

I will be exploring Fensory a whole lot this week.
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
我刚刚给人工智能交易代理分配了第一个交易任务。

我的指示很简单：使用 EMA 交叉构建 BTC 趋势跟踪策略。

但接下来发生的事情比我想象的更有趣。

使用 @FensoryApp ，我通过其 AI 代理完成了策略构建过程。

它问了我以下问题：

- 资产和时间范围。
- 贸易方向和杠杆。
- 最大头寸规模。
- 止损配置。

我选择了 BTC 永续合约、1 小时时间框架、1 倍杠杆、最高 10 美元头寸和 2 倍 ATR 止损。

然后是回测。

在过去 90 天内，该策略生成了 21 个假设头寸。

其中只有2家盈利，19家亏损。

总体模拟结果为-9.3%，最大回撤为18.11%。

这不完全是我所希望的结果。

但这是有趣的部分。

该代理人并没有简单地展示结果，而是指出了较高的止损命中率（76%），并建议在相同的美元风险下探索更广泛的止损。

它甚至提出设计该战略的第二个版本。

没有执行任何实时交易。

这是历史回测，而不是真实的交易结果。

这不是我第一次交易，但这是我第一次真正通过人工智能代理提出交易想法，而且我已经看到了可能性。

不是因为它神奇地知道如何赚钱，

但因为它可以帮助将想法转化为规则，所以测试这些规则并确定可能需要改进的领域。

本周我将大量探索 Fensory。

viral_posts.full_text_en:
i wouldn't trust an AI agent with my entire portfolio just because it has a good-looking interface or promises to make smart decisions.

personally, i'd want to use it for a while before relying on it.

i'd pay attention to the small things first.

does it follow my instructions consistently? does it make its actions easy to understand? does the experience feel predictable, or am i constantly wondering what it's doing?

that's the kind of experience i want to see from @meetmotes.

i don't think people will start trusting AI agents simply because the technology becomes more advanced.

they'll trust them after using them repeatedly and seeing that they actually do what they're supposed to do.

for me, that's how an AI agent earns a place in someone's financial routine.

not through big promises, but through everyday reliability.

viral_posts.full_text_en:
WTF IS META DOING.

Meta's Muse AI agent has 10M+ downloads, is the #2 free app on the iPhone App Store, and it's reading end-to-end encrypted Signal messages and dropping bank balances into random chats.

Reuters dug up internal complaints from Meta's own staff. A Meta employee got a reminder from Muse to reply to her sister on Signal even though she never granted access, and the AI Now Institute independently reproduced it.

Another employee chatting about fishing weather got hit with: "BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57." They never shared bank info with Muse. Meta called those exact numbers "hallucinations."

Earlier the Mac app read a writer's messages after being told no, and this week The Hacker News showed a malicious webpage attack that hijacks Muse to steal private chats and memories.

Delete this spyware or run your agents locally where you can see what they touch.
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
WTF 这是元行为。

Meta 的 Muse AI 代理下载量超过 1000 万次，是 iPhone 应用商店中排名第二的免费应用程序，它可以读取端到端加密的 Signal 消息，并将银行余额放入随机聊天中。

路透社从 Meta 自己的员工那里挖掘出了内部投诉。一名 Meta 员工收到了 Muse 的提醒，要求她在 Signal 上回复她的姐姐，尽管她从未授予访问权限，AI Now Institute 独立复制了该信息。

另一名员工在谈论钓鱼天气时遭到了这样的回应：“顺便说一句，两次银行更新，您的第一资本余额为 2722.58 美元，您的嘉信理财余额为 5899.57 美元。”他们从未与 Muse 分享银行信息。梅塔将这些确切的数字称为“幻觉”。

早些时候，Mac 应用程序在被拒绝后读取了作者的消息，本周《黑客新闻》展示了一次恶意网页攻击，该攻击劫持 Muse 以窃取私人聊天和记忆。
